sections.heading: Why scale may not create a moat
sections.content: Tavel contrasts Mechanical Turk with Airbnb, whose varied listings cater to different preferences, so additional supply can keep improving the customer experience. In a labor marketplace, the next worker may be interchangeable with existing workers; she says having 5 million Turkers rather than 100,000 probably would not materially change the experience for someone using the service.

sections.heading: Why competitors can copy it
sections.content: Because it takes relatively little homogeneous supply to create a good-enough experience for a market segment, early Mechanical Turk faced copycats and clones that could offer something comparable without accumulating the same amount of supply. That weakens the incumbent’s ability to use its scale to escape competition.

sections.heading: Why supply homogeneity weakens defensibility
sections.content: For a marketplace flywheel to strengthen with scale, more supply should make the customer experience better. Airbnb benefits from heterogeneous listings that match different preferences, but Mechanical Turk’s labor supply is comparatively homogeneous. Tavel says a customer’s experience may be much the same whether the platform has 100,000 Turkers or 5 million. Because it takes relatively little supply to offer an equally good experience to a segment of customers, competitors could copy Mechanical Turk and serve those segments without reproducing its full scale—making its lead harder to defend.
